newsitem.title: USA: BEEF--U.S. exports to Japan seen slowly rebounding.
newsitem.headline: BEEF--U.S. exports to Japan seen slowly rebounding.

text.p: U.S. beef exports to Japan may be slowly recovering after dropping sharply over the summer in the wake of a deadly outbreak of food poisoning there plus the "mad cow" scare in Europe.
"We have heard from some of our exporters that we have bottomed out and turned the corner," said Ron Willis, a beef director at the Denver-based U.S. Meat Export Federation.
However, an E.coli outbreak last week that sickened 17 people in Japan, including 15 children, could a cause a new slowdown in meat consumption there, Willis said.
The source of either the latest E.coli outbreak or the previous ones that killed 11 people and made more than 9,500 ill in Japan has not been positively identified.
U.S. meat packing giant IBP Inc reported a drop in beef exports to the Far East because of the publicity surrounding the illnesses but the drop should be temporary.
"I think the worst is behind us," said Bob Price, livestock analyst with Cargill Investor Services. "I think they (Japanese) are showing better interest for cuts that have to be cooked."
Price said that if that interest turns into sales it would be supportive to U.S. cattle prices.
The "mad cow" scare surfaced when researchers early this year said eating beef from diseased cows could possibly cause a degenerative brain disorder in humans.
"What we saw is they (Japanese) basically quit eating meat," USMEF's Willis said. "We expect August and September (beef) exports to be off 20 to 30 percent," versus a year ago.

Japan is the leading U.S. export market for beef and pork, with that country buying 661 million lbs of beef and nearly 340 million lbs of pork from January to July, 1996 versus 539 million and 188 million lbs, respectively, in the same period a year ago.
However, since July, exports have dropped.

Japan's Finance Ministry reported Monday that total beef imports were down 29.5 percent in August and pork imports down 46.5 percent from year-earlier levels. Shipments from the United States were down 34 percent for beef and 23 for pork for that period.
Pork exports were not as severely hurt because pork typically is well cooked, lessening the chance of E. coli poisoning, meat sources said.
The drop in exports has been good news for U.S. consumers. Prices for some beef cuts have dropped because beef that would normally be exported was diverted to U.S. supermarkets.
"That's one reason we have lower prices," said Kevin Bost, a market analyst for Topco Associates Inc.
Topco is a supplier of meat and other foods to supermarkets nationwide, and Bost estimated prices for some beef cuts are down five to 10 percent from a year ago.
Wholesale prices for boneless rib roasts averaged $3.60 per lb since mid-August versus $3.77 a year ago and beef sirloin prices averaged $2.62 versus $2.88.
Prices for ground beef, chuck and round cuts were up slightly from a year ago because of an overall decline in U.S. beef production and these cuts are not normally exported, he said.
